title: Unbounded partial quotients of the cube root of 2
credit: Classical question (Khintchine; Lang–Trotter 1972); framing relative to Haynes' totally real claim is new here.
premise_risks: Haynes' totally-real theorem is an unrefereed preprint since 2023; if it is wrong the 'natural frontier' framing weakens but the problem is unaffected
plain: The continued fraction of the square root of 2 is periodic, but no pattern is known in the continued fraction of the cube root of 2 = [1; 3, 1, 5, 1, 1, 4, 1, 1, 8, 1, 14, ...]. It is believed to behave like a random number and have arbitrarily large terms, but it has never been proved that its terms are unbounded. Prove that they are.
math: Let $2^{1/3}=[a_0;a_1,a_2,\ldots]$ be the simple continued fraction. Prove $\sup_n a_n=\infty$; equivalently, $2^{1/3}$ is not badly approximable: $\liminf_{q\to\infty} q\,\|q\,2^{1/3}\|=0$, where $\|\cdot\|$ is the distance to the nearest integer.
